pairs.question: q01
pairs.prompt: I use Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI on the same laptop, and every time I add an MCP server I have to hand-edit three config files in three different formats. Is there a free command-line tool that keeps one list of my MCP servers and syncs it into all three agents' configs? It should run locally with no account and leave my other settings alone.
pairs.A:
I couldn't find a single well-established tool that does exactly this. The closest fit is **sync-agents-settings**. It treats Claude Code's own config as your one list and copies those servers into Gemini CLI and Codex CLI, leaving their other settings alone. I've only read the READMEs and haven't run any of these tools. All of them are small projects with few stars, so skim the code before you let one write to your configs.

**My assumptions:** you want your user-wide configs synced (`~/.claude.json`, `~/.gemini/settings.json`, `~/.codex/config.toml`) rather than per-project files, and you have Node.js installed.

## Main recommendation: sync-agents-settings

[Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings](https://github.com/Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings), MIT license, runs locally, no account.

**Why it fits:**
- You keep adding servers the usual way (`claude mcp add …`), and Claude Code's config becomes the master list.
- It writes Gemini's JSON and Codex's TOML for you. HTTP/SSE servers are converted to a `url` entry for Codex.
- The README says existing settings stay intact (for example, a Gemini theme). It also backs up each file to `~/.sync-agents-backup/<timestamp>/` before writing.
- It has `--dry-run`, `diff` and `doctor` (checks for drift and parse errors), and it skips any agent that isn't installed.

**Limitations:**
- **It only adds servers.** It never overwrites a server that already exists in a target, and the README doesn't document any way to remove servers. If you change or delete a server in Claude Code, you'll still need to fix it by hand in the other two, or try its `reconcile` command, whose exact behaviour I couldn't confirm.
- The README only shows one `--target` per `sync` command.

**Install (needs Node 18+):**
```bash
npm install -g sync-agents-settings
# or run it without installing: npx sync-agents-settings <command>
```

**First run:**
```bash
sync-agents list                         # servers it found in Claude Code
sync-agents diff --target gemini codex   # how the others differ
sync-agents sync --target gemini --dry-run
sync-agents sync --target codex --dry-run
sync-agents sync --target gemini         # write for real (backs up first)
sync-agents sync --target codex
sync-agents doctor --target gemini codex # check for drift or parse errors
```
After that, each time you add a server: `claude mcp add …`, then run the two `sync` commands again.

## Alternatives

| Tool | Why you might pick it | Drawback |
|---|---|---|
| [mcpport](https://github.com/Abdalkaderdev/mcpport) (`npm i -g mcpport`, Node 22+) | Covers Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor. `sync` only previews unless you add `--apply`. Keeps unrelated keys, and keeps comments in Codex's TOML. Makes timestamped backups. | No separate master file: you sync from one agent to another, e.g. `mcpport sync claude gemini --apply`. 0 stars. |
| [EnjoyableWork/mcp-sync](https://github.com/EnjoyableWork/mcp-sync) (`brew install EnjoyableWork/tap/mcp-sync`) | Has its own master file (`~/.config/mcp-sync/config.json`), keeps other settings, never deletes servers on its own. | Its documented targets are Codex, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code and Kiro. **It doesn't list Claude Code or Gemini CLI.** |
| [mcp-config-manager](https://github.com/holstein13/mcp-config-manager) (Python) | Built for Claude, Gemini and Codex, with enable/disable and backups. | The Codex path in its README is `~/.codex.json`, not `config.toml`, which suggests it's out of date for current Codex. Its installer is `curl \| bash`. It doesn't say whether it keeps other settings. |
| [mcp-sync (Rust)](https://docs.rs/crate/mcp-sync/latest/source/README.md) | Master `mcp.yaml`, `--dry-run`, `--clean` to remove servers that aren't in the master file. | Doesn't support Gemini CLI. |
| [Ruler](https://github.com/intellectronica/ruler) (~3k stars) | The most established tool here. Its `ruler.toml` keeps one MCP list for Claude, Codex and Gemini. | **Per-project only.** It never writes MCP config outside the project folder, so it doesn't fit if you want user-wide settings. |

**Bottom line:** use sync-agents-settings if you're happy for Claude Code to hold the master list. Try mcpport if you'd rather see a preview before every write and want Codex's TOML comments kept. Use Ruler only if you manage MCP servers per project. Whichever you choose, back up the three config files yourself before the first real sync.

Sources:
- [sync-agents-settings](https://github.com/Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings)
- [mcpport](https://github.com/Abdalkaderdev/mcpport)
- [EnjoyableWork/mcp-sync](https://github.com/EnjoyableWork/mcp-sync)
- [holstein13/mcp-config-manager](https://github.com/holstein13/mcp-config-manager)
- [mcp-sync (docs.rs)](https://docs.rs/crate/mcp-sync/latest/source/README.md)
- [intellectronica/ruler](https://github.com/intellectronica/ruler)
- [ejfn/mcp-sync](https://github.com/ejfn/mcp-sync) (appeared in search, but the repo returned 404)
pairs.B:
I recommend **mcpshare**. It's free and open source, runs locally with no account, and supports Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI. It's the closest match to what you asked for: you keep one master list of MCP servers, and `mcpshare sync` writes it into each agent's config in that agent's own format. According to its README, it replaces only the MCP section of each file, so your other settings stay. That includes Claude's state in `~/.claude.json`, Gemini's other settings, and the non-MCP sections of Codex's TOML file. It skips config files it can't parse instead of overwriting them.

**Things to know before you use it**
- [source], the tool-recommendation service I checked, had tested none of these tools. My information comes from a web search and each project's README. I haven't run any of them.
- mcpshare is a small, young project: about 19 commits, no tagged releases, and no license shown on its GitHub page. It has **no dry-run or backup option**, so back up your configs before your first sync.
- It has no `add` command. To add a server, you edit the master `mcp.json` file and then run `sync`.

## Install (macOS)
It's a Python tool installed with `uv`. I'm assuming you have Homebrew.
```bash
brew install uv                                            # skip if you already have uv
uv tool install git+https://github.com/eggboy/mcpshare.git
mcpshare --help                                            # check that it installed
```
Upgrade later with `uv tool upgrade mcpshare`.

## First run
1. **Back up your current configs:**
   ```bash
   mkdir -p ~/mcp-backup
   cp ~/.claude.json ~/.gemini/settings.json ~/.codex/config.toml ~/mcp-backup/
   ```
2. **Create mcpshare's config:** `mcpshare init` creates `~/.config/mcpshare/config.yaml` and the folder for the master list.
3. **Edit `config.yaml`.** By default it imports existing servers from VS Code and Copilot, so point it at the agents you use instead. The README names the keys `source`, `init-source`, `mode` and `targets`, with a `path` for each target. I'm guessing at the exact layout, so compare it with the file `init` creates:
   ```yaml
   init-source: [claude]        # import your existing servers from Claude Code
   targets:
     claude: { path: ~/.claude }
     codex:  { path: ~/.codex }
     gemini: { path: ~/.gemini }
   ```
4. **Import your current servers:** `mcpshare pull` copies them into the master `mcp.json` and doesn't write to any agent's config.
5. **Check before writing:** `mcpshare status` shows the master servers, the targets and any disabled servers.
6. **Sync:** `mcpshare sync`. Then compare each file with your backup, for example `diff ~/mcp-backup/config.toml ~/.codex/config.toml`, to confirm only the MCP sections changed.
7. **From now on:** add the server to the master `mcp.json` and run `mcpshare sync`. To turn a server off for one agent, use `mcpshare disable --servers <name> --ide gemini`.

## Other options
- **mcpport** (MIT license, needs Node 22+) has the safety features mcpshare lacks. Sync is a dry run unless you add `--apply`, it makes a timestamped `.bak` copy before every write, and it keeps comments and unrelated settings. It has no master list, though: you use one agent (say Claude Code) as the source and copy from it. For example, run `npx mcpport sync claude codex`, check the output, then run it again with `--apply`, and do the same for `gemini`. One catch: if your Gemini `settings.json` contains comments, mcpport reads it but never writes to it. Choose mcpport over mcpshare if you'd rather have dry runs and backups than a separate master list.
- **sync-agents-settings** also syncs from Claude Code to Gemini and Codex, and has `diff` and `doctor` commands. I didn't read its documentation closely.

Sources:
- [eggboy/mcpshare](https://github.com/eggboy/mcpshare)
- [Abdalkaderdev/mcpport](https://github.com/Abdalkaderdev/mcpport)
- [Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings](https://github.com/Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings)
- [holstein13/mcp-config-manager](https://github.com/holstein13/mcp-config-manager)
- [EnjoyableWork/mcp-sync](https://github.com/EnjoyableWork/mcp-sync)

pairs.question: q02
pairs.prompt: Before I paste server logs into an AI chat, I want to automatically scrub API keys, tokens, email addresses and IP addresses out of them. Is there a free, open-source command-line filter (stdin to stdout) that does this entirely on my Linux machine, without me having to write the regexes myself?
pairs.A:
I recommend **leakguard**. It's a small Rust command-line tool that reads stdin and writes redacted text to stdout. It runs entirely on your machine, needs no network, and is MIT/Apache-2.0 licensed. You don't write any regexes: it already detects emails, IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, JWTs, AWS, GitHub, Slack, Stripe, Google and OpenAI keys, Azure connection strings, PEM private keys, passwords inside URLs, and more. Version 1.0.0 came out on 2026-10-06 and it has about 74k downloads on crates.io.

I haven't installed or run it. [source], the tool-recommendation service I checked first, had no tested tool for this job. Everything below comes from leakguard's README and its crates.io page.

## Install (Linux)

You need a Rust toolchain (Rust 1.70 or newer). If you don't have one, install it with your distro's package manager or with rustup:

```bash
# Option A: distro package (Debian/Ubuntu example)
sudo apt install cargo

# Option B: rustup (official installer; read the script first if you prefer)
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh

# Then:
cargo install leakguard
```

The binary goes into `~/.cargo/bin`, so make sure that folder is on your `PATH`.

## First run

```bash
# See what it detects
leakguard --list-kinds

# Scrub a log and copy to clipboard for pasting (X11 / Wayland)
leakguard < server.log | xclip -selection clipboard
leakguard < server.log | wl-copy

# Check what was redacted (summary goes to stderr)
leakguard --stats server.log > clean.log

# Live tail
tail -f app.log | leakguard
```

By default each match is replaced with a label such as `[REDACTED:EMAIL]`. Some useful options:
- `--mask partial --keep 4` keeps the last 4 characters, which helps you tell values apart.
- `--ignore 10.0.0.1,test@example.com` leaves values you know are safe untouched.
- `--redact-word AcmeCorp` or `--redact-literal "..."` also removes your own hostnames, customer names and similar terms.
- `--without credit_card` helps with logs full of numbers. Some long timestamps pass the card checksum and get redacted by mistake.
- `--check` exits with code 1 if anything sensitive is found, so you can use it as a "safe to paste?" check.

## Important limitation

The command-line tool doesn't do high-entropy detection (spotting random-looking strings); only the library has that. In practice it catches tokens with known formats but can **miss custom or unprefixed secrets**, like `Authorization: Bearer <opaque>` or `api_key=abc123...` from your own services. Always look over the output before pasting, and add `--redact-literal` for any secrets you know about. The README calls the tool "best-effort" and says its detectors are conservative.

## Alternatives (not checked in detail)

- **cleansh** (Rust, `cargo install cleansh`): reads stdin and masks emails, IPs, JWT/AWS/GCP tokens, SSH keys and hex secrets. It's newer and much less used (about 2.7k downloads, last release December 2025).
- **ferret-scan** (Go): `--stdin --enable-redaction` writes redacted text to stdout and scores matches by context. It may catch more generic secrets, but it's a bigger tool.
- **redactor** (its30NA) and **redactcli** (PyPI): both are built specifically for cleaning text before pasting it into an AI chat. They're small projects whose quality I haven't checked.

Sources:
- [leakguard on GitHub](https://github.com/ptukovar/leakguard) · [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/crate/leakguard/latest/source/src/bin/leakguard.rs) · [crates.io API](https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/leakguard)
- [cleansh](https://docs.rs/crate/cleansh/0.1.4/source/src/main.rs) · [crates.io API](https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/cleansh)
- [ferret-scan](https://github.com/orshih6/ferret-scan)
- [redactor](https://github.com/its30NA/redactor)
- [redactcli](https://pypi.org/project/redactcli/)
- [rog7/redact](https://github.com/rog7/redact)
- [redactscan PR #8](https://github.com/boktavec/redactscan/pull/8)
pairs.B:
**My pick: [leakguard](https://github.com/ptukovar/leakguard).** It's a small Rust command-line tool, dual-licensed MIT/Apache-2.0, with no dependencies. It reads from stdin, writes the redacted text to stdout, and runs entirely on your machine. The patterns are already built in, so you don't write any regexes.

**What it catches by default:** emails, IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, JWTs, AWS, Google, Stripe and OpenAI keys, GitHub, Slack, Telegram and Discord tokens, passwords inside URLs, Azure connection strings, PEM private keys, plus credit cards, SSNs, MAC addresses and IBANs. It can also flag any random-looking string as a possible secret (the generic "high-entropy" detector), but that's off by default and you have to turn it on.

## Install

I'm assuming you have the Rust toolchain or are willing to install it. The tool is installed through Cargo, Rust's package manager.

```bash
# Only if you don't already have cargo (Rust's official installer):
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"

cargo install leakguard
leakguard --list-kinds    # shows the exact names of the things it can detect
```

## First run

```bash
# 1. Test on a sample first and compare the output with the original
leakguard --stats < server.log > server.redacted.log
diff <(head -200 server.log) <(head -200 server.redacted.log) | less

# 2. Normal use: pipe a log through it
journalctl -u myapp --since "1 hour ago" | leakguard > for-ai.txt
tail -n 500 /var/log/nginx/error.log | leakguard

# 3. Also scrub your own internal hostnames or names it can't know about
cat app.log | leakguard --redact-word mycorp.internal --redact-word db-prod-01
```

Use `--only` and `--without` to choose which patterns run, and `--mask` to change how redacted values look. To turn on the random-string detector, find its exact name in `--list-kinds` and add it with `--only`. If you do that, list the default kinds you still want as well. I haven't checked whether `--only` replaces the default set or adds to it, so look at the output to be sure. `--check` exits with code 1 if it finds anything, which is handy in scripts.

## Caveats

- **It's young.** Version 1.0.0 came out on 2026-10-06 and looks like a one-person project. Read through the source before you trust it, and pin the version.
- **Pattern matching has gaps.** It will miss secrets in formats it doesn't know: custom session IDs, internal hostnames, usernames, and keys inside unusual config formats. Always skim the output before you paste it. `--redact-word` handles known internal strings.
- **IPs:** it redacts all of them, including harmless ones like `127.0.0.1`. If you want to keep some, `--ignore` lets you allowlist values.

## Alternatives

- **[cleansh](https://docs.rs/crate/cleansh/latest)** (Rust, MIT/Apache-2.0): `cargo install cleansh`, then `cat app.log | cleansh sanitize`. It covers similar ground, also shortens home paths to `~/`, and has an opt-in random-string detector (`--engine entropy`). It pulls in an HTTP library and has inactive paid-service stubs. If you need a guarantee that nothing leaves the machine, check the source or run it with no network access.
- **[hexredact](https://github.com/happygream/hexredact):** replaces each value with a token, and the same value always gets the same token. That lets the AI still follow, say, "IP_3" through the whole log, and you can reverse it afterwards.
- **[rog7/redact](https://github.com/rog7/redact)** and **[local-redact](https://github.com/sumankrsh/local-redact)** (Python): simpler, smaller pattern sets.
- Gitleaks and TruffleHog are better known, but they report secrets rather than filtering text through, so they don't fit stdin-to-stdout use.

I didn't install or run any of these. The details above come from their docs.rs and GitHub pages.

Sources:
- [leakguard on docs.rs](https://docs.rs/crate/leakguard/latest) / [source](https://docs.rs/crate/leakguard/latest/source/src/bin/leakguard.rs)
- [cleansh on docs.rs](https://docs.rs/crate/cleansh/latest) / [cleansh crate docs](https://docs.rs/cleansh/0.1.7/i686-unknown-linux-gnu/cleansh/)
- [hexredact](https://github.com/happygream/hexredact)
- [rog7/redact](https://github.com/rog7/redact)
- [local-redact](https://github.com/sumankrsh/local-redact)

pairs.question: q03
pairs.prompt: I regularly get 2-5 GB CSV exports and need to filter rows, pick columns, and do group-by counts from the terminal on Linux. pandas is too slow and memory-hungry, and awk breaks on quoted fields that contain commas and line breaks. What free, open-source tool should I use? It must be a single binary or a distro package, with no Python, Java or Node runtime.
pairs.A:
I recommend **DuckDB**, used through its command-line tool. It's free and open source (MIT) and comes as one standalone binary with no runtime to install. It reads RFC 4180 CSV correctly, including quoted fields that contain commas and line breaks. It uses all your CPU cores and works through the file in chunks, so a 5 GB file doesn't need 5 GB of RAM. Filtering rows, picking columns and group-by counts all fit in one SQL query.

If you'd rather chain small Unix-style commands than write SQL, use **qsv** instead (details below).

I checked [source]'s tested catalog and none of its tools matched this request. The advice below is from general knowledge, and I haven't installed or run any of these here.

## 1. DuckDB CLI (main recommendation)

**Install (one binary, x86_64):**
```bash
# Option A: download from GitHub Releases
wget https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/releases/latest/download/duckdb_cli-linux-amd64.zip
unzip duckdb_cli-linux-amd64.zip        # gives you a single file: ./duckdb
install -m 755 duckdb ~/.local/bin/     # or /usr/local/bin with sudo

# Option B: official install script (read it before piping it into sh)
curl https://install.duckdb.org | sh
```
On ARM, use `duckdb_cli-linux-arm64.zip` instead. Check the install with `duckdb --version`.

**First run:**
```bash
# Look at the columns and types DuckDB detects
duckdb -c "DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM read_csv('big.csv');"

# Filter, pick columns, write a new CSV
duckdb -c "COPY (SELECT id, status, amount FROM read_csv('big.csv')
                 WHERE status = 'ERROR' AND amount > 100)
           TO 'filtered.csv' (HEADER);"

# Group-by count
duckdb -c "SELECT status, count(*) AS n FROM read_csv('big.csv')
           GROUP BY status ORDER BY n DESC;"
```
**Tips:**
- If type detection guesses wrong on messy data, use `read_csv('big.csv', all_varchar=true)` or `sample_size=-1`.
- To limit memory, add `SET memory_limit='2GB';` at the start of the command. DuckDB writes the overflow to temporary files on disk instead of crashing.
- If you'll query the same file many times, convert it once: `COPY (FROM 'big.csv') TO 'big.parquet';`. Later queries on the Parquet file run much faster.

## 2. qsv (if you prefer command pipelines)

qsv is a Rust tool that continues the older, unmaintained `xsv` project. It's released under MIT/Unlicense and ships static builds (musl) that run on any Linux distro.

**Install:** On the GitHub Releases page for `dathere/qsv`, download `qsv-<version>-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.zip`. Unzip it and put `qsv` on your PATH. Check the install with `qsv --version`.

**First run:**
```bash
qsv index big.csv          # optional; builds an index that makes count, slice and frequency much faster
qsv count big.csv
qsv search -s status '^ERROR$' big.csv | qsv select id,status,amount > filtered.csv
qsv frequency -s status --limit 0 big.csv     # group-by counts
```

## 3. Miller (if it must be a distro package)

Miller handles quoted fields correctly, including ones with line breaks inside them. It's in the standard repos:
- Debian/Ubuntu: `sudo apt install miller`
- Fedora: `sudo dnf install miller`
- Arch: `sudo pacman -S miller`

Try it with `mlr --icsv --opprint count -g status big.csv`. Miller is slower than the two tools above at 2–5 GB, and commands like `sort` load all the data into memory. That's why I rank it third.

**My assumptions:** You're on x86_64 Linux and allowed to put a binary in `~/.local/bin`. The column names in the examples (`status`, `amount`, `id`) are placeholders for your own.

**Bottom line:** For one-off filtering and group-by counts, DuckDB is the fastest and easiest of these. Add qsv if you like building up pipelines command by command.
pairs.B:
# Use qsv

Install **qsv** ([github.com/dathere/qsv](https://github.com/dathere/qsv)). It is the maintained successor to BurntSushi's `xsv`, written in Rust, and released under MIT/Unlicense. It ships as one static binary with no runtime. Its CSV parser follows RFC 4180, so quoted fields that contain commas and line breaks are handled correctly. It streams the file instead of loading it into memory, and once you build an index it uses all your cores. A 2–5 GB file should be no problem.

My assumptions: x86_64 Linux, and UTF-8 CSV with standard double-quote escaping. I didn't run anything on this machine.

## Install

1. Open the [releases page](https://github.com/dathere/qsv/releases/latest) and download the asset named `qsv-<version>-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.zip`. The musl build is fully static, so it runs on any distro. Use the `aarch64` build on ARM.
2. Unzip it and install it:
   ```bash
   unzip qsv-*-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.zip -d qsv-dl
   install -m 755 qsv-dl/qsv ~/.local/bin/    # or sudo install ... /usr/local/bin/
   qsv --version
   ```
   The zip also contains `qsvlite` and `qsvdp`, which are smaller variants. You only need `qsv`.

qsv is in Homebrew, Nix, Arch (AUR) and Scoop, but it generally isn't in the Debian, Ubuntu or Fedora repos. If you need a distro package, see Miller below.

## First run

```bash
qsv index big.csv                 # one-time; writes big.csv.idx, makes count/frequency/stats fast + parallel
qsv headers big.csv               # list column names with their positions
qsv count big.csv                 # row count (instant once indexed)

# Pick columns
qsv select id,status,country big.csv > slim.csv

# Filter rows (regex on one column), then pick columns
qsv search -s status '^shipped$' big.csv | qsv select id,country,amount > shipped.csv

# Group-by count on one column (all values, sorted by count)
qsv frequency -s country --limit 0 big.csv

# Multi-column group-by, or filter+group in one step (SQL via the built-in Polars engine)
qsv sqlp big.csv "SELECT country, status, COUNT(*) AS n
                  FROM _t_1 WHERE amount > 100
                  GROUP BY country, status ORDER BY n DESC"
```

A few other commands that help: `qsv stats big.csv` profiles each column, `qsv slice -l 20 big.csv | qsv table` gives a quick look at the data, and `qsv sort` and `qsv dedup` do what their names say. `qsv --list` shows every command.

## Alternatives

- **DuckDB CLI** (MIT license, single binary, `duckdb_cli-linux-amd64.zip` on its GitHub releases page). Pick this if most of your work is SQL-style grouping, joins or aggregations. It's very fast, multithreaded, and runs out-of-core:
  ```bash
  duckdb -c "SELECT country, status, count(*) n FROM read_csv('big.csv') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n DESC"
  ```
- **Miller (`mlr`)** (BSD license, single Go binary). Pick this if you must install from your distro's repos: `apt install miller` or `dnf install miller`. It's slower than qsv or DuckDB on files this big, but it parses CSV correctly and its syntax is friendly:
  ```bash
  mlr --icsv --opprint filter '$amount > 100' then count -g country,status big.csv
  ```
- **Avoid plain `xsv`.** It works, but it's no longer maintained, and qsv covers everything it does.

In short: use qsv for everyday filter, select and count work, and add DuckDB when the queries get complex.

pairs.question: q04
pairs.prompt: Our 4-person team shares .env files over chat, which is obviously bad. We want to commit the secrets to our git repo encrypted, let each developer decrypt with their own key, and be able to cut someone off cleanly when they leave the team. No hosted secrets service and no server to run, and it has to be free and open source. We use macOS and Linux.
pairs.A:
# Recommendation: SOPS + age

Use **[SOPS](https://github.com/getsops/sops)** to encrypt the files and **[age](https://github.com/FiloSottile/age)** for each developer's key. Both are free, open source (MPL-2.0 and BSD-3), run on macOS and Linux, and need no server or hosted service.

How it fits what you asked for:

- **Encrypted files in git.** You commit a file such as `secrets.enc.env`. SOPS encrypts only the values and leaves the key names readable, so `git diff` shows which variable changed without showing the secret.
- **Each developer has their own key.** Every person makes an age keypair and you list all four public keys in `.sops.yaml`. Anyone on that list can decrypt with their own private key. Nobody shares a password.
- **Cutting someone off.** Remove their public key, re-encrypt with a new data key, and change the actual secrets. Step 7 explains why you have to change the secrets too.

I wrote this from memory and haven't run anything on your machines. I'm assuming SOPS 3.9 or newer, which has the `sops encrypt`, `sops decrypt`, `sops edit` and `sops rotate` subcommands. On older versions the equivalents are `-e`, `-d`, plain `sops file` and `-r`.

---

## Install (each developer)

**macOS (Homebrew):**
```sh
brew install sops age
```

**Linux:**
```sh
# age is in most current distro repos (Debian 12+, Ubuntu 22.04+, Fedora, Arch)
sudo apt install age        # or: dnf install age / pacman -S age

# sops: download the binary from https://github.com/getsops/sops/releases
# (pick the linux.amd64 or linux.arm64 asset and check it against the published checksums file)
curl -LO https://github.com/getsops/sops/releases/download/vX.Y.Z/sops-vX.Y.Z.linux.amd64
sudo install -m 755 sops-vX.Y.Z.linux.amd64 /usr/local/bin/sops
```
Arch also has `pacman -S sops`, and Homebrew on Linux works too.

Check with `sops --version` and `age --version`.

## First run

**1. Each developer creates a key** (one time, on their own machine):
```sh
# Linux default location:
mkdir -p ~/.config/sops/age
age-keygen -o ~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt

# macOS default location:
mkdir -p "$HOME/Library/Application Support/sops/age"
age-keygen -o "$HOME/Library/Application Support/sops/age/keys.txt"
```
If you'd rather use the same path on both systems, set `export SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE=~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt` in your shell profile.

The command prints a **public key** (`age1...`). Each person posts that public key in chat, which is safe because it's public. The private key file never leaves their machine. Back it up in your password manager.

**2. Add `.sops.yaml` to the root of the repo:**
```yaml
creation_rules:
  - path_regex: \.enc\.env$
    age: >-
      age1alice...,
      age1bob...,
      age1carol...,
      age1dave...
```

**3. Keep plaintext out of git.** Add this to `.gitignore`:
```
.env
.env.*
!*.enc.env
```

**4. Encrypt the current `.env` once and commit it:**
```sh
sops encrypt .env > secrets.enc.env      # the .env extension makes sops use dotenv format
git add .sops.yaml secrets.enc.env .gitignore
git commit -m "Add encrypted secrets"
```
After that, delete the copies of the `.env` that went around in chat, and plan to rotate those secrets because they've already been exposed.

**5. Daily use:**
```sh
sops edit secrets.enc.env                      # opens $EDITOR and re-encrypts when you save
sops decrypt secrets.enc.env > .env            # if your tooling needs a plain .env file
sops exec-env secrets.enc.env 'npm run dev'    # or skip the file and inject the vars into a process
```

**6. Adding a new teammate:** add their `age1...` key to `.sops.yaml`, then someone who already has access runs:
```sh
sops updatekeys -y secrets.enc.env
git commit -am "Grant access to <name>"
```

**7. Offboarding:**
```sh
# 1. remove their public key from .sops.yaml
sops updatekeys -y secrets.enc.env   # takes them off the recipient list
sops rotate -i secrets.enc.env       # makes a new data key
# 2. change the real secrets (API keys, DB passwords) at each provider
sops edit secrets.enc.env            # paste in the new values
git commit -am "Revoke <name>, rotate secrets"
```
**Step 2 is required.** Git history still holds the old encrypted file, and the person leaving can decrypt it with their key. Any secret they could read before should be treated as known to them. Encryption tooling can't fix that; you have to change the credentials at the source.

---

## Other tips

- **Per-environment access:** use separate files such as `dev.enc.env` and `prod.enc.env`, each with its own `creation_rules` entry, so prod can have a shorter recipient list.
- **CI:** create a separate age key for CI, add it as a recipient, and store the private key in the CI system's secret store as `SOPS_AGE_KEY`.
- **SSH keys:** age can also encrypt to existing `ssh-ed25519` public keys, but separate age keys are simpler and keep your SSH and secrets keys apart.

## Alternatives I'd skip

| Tool | Why not first choice |
|---|---|
| git-crypt | Needs GPG and encrypts whole files, so diffs are useless. Removing a user is awkward. |
| git-secret | GPG-based and clunkier to use. |
| transcrypt | Everyone shares one password, so you can't remove a single person. |
| dotenvx | Works well, but each environment has one shared private key, not one key per person. |

Sources:
- https://github.com/getsops/sops
- https://github.com/FiloSottile/age

pairs.prompt: 我平常用 pandoc 把 Word 檔轉成 Markdown 給 AI 讀，但它不能讀 PDF，而我們很多規格書都是 PDF。想找一個在 Linux 終端機就能用的工具，PDF 和 Word 都能轉成 Markdown，PDF 裡的表格要保留成表格，標題層級也要正確。公司文件不能上傳到雲端，只能在本機跑，電腦也沒有 GPU。免費最好，買斷也可以，但不要訂閱制。
pairs.A:
我推薦用 **Docling**（IBM 開源，MIT 授權，免費）。它是 Python 寫的命令列工具，PDF 和 Word 都能轉成 Markdown。PDF 裡的表格會轉成 Markdown 表格，有 `--heading-hierarchy` 選項來還原標題層級。只用 CPU 就能跑，第一次下載完模型之後就可以完全離線使用。

先說清楚：[source] 查了 208 個工具，沒有找到它實際測試過、又同時符合你所有條件的。所以下面的建議和指令都是根據我自己的了解和 Docling 官方文件，**[source] 沒有替它做過安裝測試**。

**我的假設：** 你的 Linux 有 Python 3.10 以上；規格書大多是軟體輸出的 PDF，不是掃描檔。

## 為什麼選 Docling

- **表格：** 用專門的表格辨識模型（TableFormer）找出表格結構，輸出成 Markdown 表格。
- **標題層級：** 這是 Docling 的已知弱點，**一定要加 `--heading-hierarchy`**。不加的話，PDF 裡所有標題都會變成同一層（全部是 `#` 或 `##`）。官方文件說這個功能預設關閉。開啟後它會參考 PDF 的書籤、章節編號（例如 3.2.1）和字體大小來判斷層級。如果規格書有書籤或編號標題，效果通常會比較好。
- **Word：** `.docx` 也能直接轉，所以 PDF 和 Word 可以用同一套流程。原本的 pandoc 也可以繼續用來轉 Word。
- **本機和沒有 GPU：** 模型很小，CPU 就能跑，但每頁要幾秒，大份規格書要多等一下。

## 安裝（Linux）

```bash
# 建一個獨立的虛擬環境
python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/docling
source ~/.venvs/docling/bin/activate

# 只用 CPU 的話，先裝 CPU 版 PyTorch，可以省下好幾 GB 的 CUDA 套件
pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
pip install docling

# 先把模型下載到本機，之後就能完全離線使用
docling-tools models download
# 模型預設放在 ~/.cache/docling/models
```

## 第一次使用

```bash
# PDF 轉 Markdown（文字型 PDF 用 --no-ocr 會比較快也比較準）
docling spec.pdf --to md --output ./out --heading-hierarchy --no-ocr --table-mode accurate

# Word 轉 Markdown
docling spec.docx --to md --output ./out

# 整個資料夾一起轉
docling ./specs/ --to md --output ./out --heading-hierarchy --no-ocr
```

**確保不會連網：** 加上 `--artifacts-path ~/.cache/docling/models`，或先執行 `export HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`。這樣它只會用本機的模型。

**建議先測試：** 挑一份表格最多、層級最深的規格書轉轉看，打開 `out/spec.md` 檢查表格和 `#`、`##`、`###` 對不對。掃描型的 PDF 就把 `--no-ocr` 拿掉，但在 CPU 上會慢很多。如果你的版本不認得 `--heading-hierarchy`，執行 `pip install -U docling` 升級。

## 其他選擇

- **MarkItDown（Microsoft，免費）：** [source] 有提到它，但同樣沒有驗證過。它轉 Word 沒問題，但 PDF 基本上只抽出純文字，**表格和標題層級都會不見**，所以不符合你的需求。
- **Marker：** PDF 轉 Markdown 品質很好，CPU 也能跑但比較慢。程式碼是 GPL 授權，模型權重對營收較高的公司有商用限制。公司內部使用前要先看清楚授權，所以我把它排在 Docling 後面。

Sources:
- [Docling – heading levels](https://docling-project.github.io/docling/usage/heading_levels/)
- [Docling heading_levels example](https://docling-project.github.io/docling/examples/heading_levels.py)
- [Docling discussion #1170（標題全部變成 ## 的問題）](https://github.com/docling-project/docling/discussions/1170)
- [md-reheader（第三方標題層級修復工具）](https://pypi.org/project/md-reheader/)

pairs.prompt: We have an internal REST API described by an OpenAPI 3 spec, and I want my AI coding agents to call it as MCP tools. Is there a free, open-source tool that turns the spec into a working MCP server I can run locally, without writing the server code by hand and without a hosted service or account? It should forward the agents' tool calls to our API's base URL.
pairs.A:
My recommendation is **`@ivotoby/openapi-mcp-server`** ([ivo-toby/mcp-openapi-server](https://github.com/ivo-toby/mcp-openapi-server)). It's MIT-licensed and runs locally with `npx`. You point it at your spec and your API's base URL, and it turns each operation into an MCP tool. When an agent calls a tool, it sends the HTTP request to that base URL. You don't write any server code and you don't need an account.

**My assumptions:** you have Node.js 18 or newer, your spec is JSON or YAML (a local file or a URL), and your API uses header-based auth such as a bearer token or API key. I haven't run any of this on your machine. The flags below come from the project's current README.

## Install and first run

**1. Install.** Nothing to install globally. `npx -y` downloads and runs the package. If you want a fixed version for reproducibility, pin one, e.g. `@ivotoby/openapi-mcp-server@<version>`, and check npm for the latest.

**2. Smoke-test it with the MCP Inspector** before connecting any agents:
```bash
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector \
  npx -y @ivotoby/openapi-mcp-server \
    --api-base-url https://internal-api.example.corp \
    --openapi-spec ./openapi.yaml \
    --headers "Authorization:Bearer $INTERNAL_API_TOKEN"
```
In the Inspector UI, connect and open **Tools**. Check that your operations appear, then call a harmless GET and confirm it reaches your API.

**3. Connect your agent.** Stdio is the default transport.

- **Claude Code:**
  ```bash
  claude mcp add internal-api \
    -e API_BASE_URL=https://internal-api.example.corp \
    -e OPENAPI_SPEC_PATH=/abs/path/openapi.yaml \
    -e API_HEADERS="Authorization:Bearer YOUR_TOKEN" \
    -- npx -y @ivotoby/openapi-mcp-server
  ```
- **Any JSON-configured client** (Claude Desktop, Cursor, etc.):
  ```json
  {
    "mcpServers": {
      "internal-api": {
        "command": "npx",
        "args": ["-y", "@ivotoby/openapi-mcp-server"],
        "env": {
          "API_BASE_URL": "https://internal-api.example.corp",
          "OPENAPI_SPEC_PATH": "/abs/path/openapi.yaml",
          "API_HEADERS": "Authorization:Bearer YOUR_TOKEN"
        }
      }
    }
  }
  ```
- **Several agents sharing one server:** run it over HTTP instead. Add `--transport http --port 3000` and point the clients at `http://127.0.0.1:3000/mcp`. The health check is at `/health`, and the server binds to 127.0.0.1 by default.

## Settings worth knowing
- **Limit what agents can do.** By default every operation becomes a tool. You can narrow that with `--tag`, `--exclude-tag`, `--tool`, `--resource <path-prefix>`, or `--operation get`. For example, `--operation get` makes the agents read-only until you trust the setup.
- **Big specs:** `--tools dynamic` gives agents a few tools for discovering and calling endpoints, instead of hundreds of separate tools that fill up their context.
- **Internal TLS:** `--ca-cert` adds your corporate CA, and `--client-cert`/`--client-key` handle mTLS. Use this rather than `--reject-unauthorized false`.
- **Keep tokens out of committed config.** Use environment variables or your client's secret handling. Also note that verbose logging is on by default.

## Alternatives
- **[`mcp-openapi-proxy`](https://pypi.org/project/mcp-openapi-proxy/)** (Python, MIT): run it with `uvx mcp-openapi-proxy`. It's configured with `OPENAPI_SPEC_URL`, which can be a URL or `file://` path, plus `SERVER_URL_OVERRIDE` for your base URL, `API_KEY`, and `TOOL_WHITELIST`. Choose this if your team prefers Python. Option names have changed between releases, so check the [README](https://github.com/matthewhand/mcp-openapi-proxy) first.
- **FastMCP's `FastMCP.from_openapi(...)`** (Python): about 10 lines of code. Use it if you later need custom auth or want to reshape responses.
- **`openapi-mcp-generator`**: generates a TypeScript server project from the spec instead of proxying at runtime. That's useful if you want code you own and can edit, but you then have to maintain the generated code.

Sources:
- [ivo-toby/mcp-openapi-server (GitHub)](https://github.com/ivo-toby/mcp-openapi-server)
- [mcp-openapi-proxy on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/mcp-openapi-proxy/0.1.1741466171/)

## Main recommendation: Bruno (MIT-licensed, offline, no account)

- **Git-friendly files:** each request is one plain-text file (`.bru`) inside a normal folder. You commit the folder to your repo, and each changed request shows up as a small, readable diff. Newer versions also offer a YAML-based format.
- **Works offline:** the desktop app has no cloud workspace and needs no sign-in.
- **CI:** the `bru` CLI runs the same files on Linux. If any assertion fails, it exits with a non-zero code, so the build fails. It can also write JUnit reports.
- **Cost:** the core app and CLI are free and open source. There's an optional paid "Golden Edition", but you don't need it for this.

### Install (Mac)
```bash
brew install --cask bruno          # desktop app
npm install -g @usebruno/cli       # CLI (needs Node 18+), command is `bru`
```

### First run
1. Open Bruno, click **Create Collection**, and pick a folder inside your repo, e.g. `api-tests/`.
2. Add a request. Bruno saves it as a file like this:
   ```
   meta { name: Get user  type: http  seq: 1 }

   get {
     url: {{baseUrl}}/users/1
   }

   assert {
     res.status: eq 200
     res.body.id: eq 1
   }

   tests {
     test("has email", function() {
       expect(res.getBody().email).to.be.a("string");
     });
   }
   ```
3. Create an environment (stored as `environments/ci.bru`) that sets `baseUrl`. Keep secrets out of git: reference them as `{{process.env.API_TOKEN}}` and put the real values in a `.env` file listed in `.gitignore`.
4. Run it locally the same way CI will:
   ```bash
   cd api-tests
   bru run --env ci
   ```
5. CI step, shown for GitHub Actions (other CI systems work the same way):
   ```yaml
   - run: npm install -g @usebruno/cli
   - run: bru run --env ci --reporter-junit results.xml
     working-directory: api-tests
     env:
       API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }}
   ```
   The reporter flag has changed between CLI versions (older versions used `--output results.xml --format junit`). Run `bru run --help` on the version you install to confirm. Also pin the CLI version in CI so local and CI runs behave the same.

## Option 2: Hurl (Apache-2.0, CLI only)
Hurl suits you if you don't need a desktop app. Each `.hurl` file is a plain-text list of requests with assertions written underneath. It's a single fast binary written in Rust (no Node needed), and its files diff very cleanly.
```bash
brew install hurl
hurl --test --report-junit results.xml tests/*.hurl
```
Example file:
```
GET {{base_url}}/users/1
HTTP 200
[Asserts]
jsonpath "$.id" == 1
```
On Linux CI, use the `.deb` package, the release tarball or the Docker image `ghcr.io/orange-opensource/hurl`.

## Other options
- **httpYac:** runs standard `.http` / `.rest` files. It has a VS Code extension and a CLI (`httpyac send --all`) that works in CI. It's a good fit if your team already writes `.http` files.

**Bottom line:** choose Bruno if people want a Postman-style app. Choose Hurl if everyone is comfortable in the terminal and you want the simplest CI setup.

pairs.A:
# Recommendation: Colima + the open-source Docker CLI

**Use [Colima](https://github.com/abiosoft/colima) (MIT license) with the Homebrew `docker`, `docker-compose`, and `docker-buildx` packages.** Colima runs a small Linux VM with the real Docker Engine (Moby) inside it, using Apple's Virtualization.framework. The Docker CLI and Compose are Apache-2.0 and free to use at any company size. Only Docker Desktop has the paid license. So your existing `docker ...` and `docker compose ...` commands, scripts and compose files keep working as they are, and arm64 images run natively.

**My assumptions:** you have Homebrew, macOS 13 or later, and you're fine re-pulling images. Images and volumes stored in Docker Desktop don't carry over.

## Install

1. **Quit and uninstall Docker Desktop first.** Its `/usr/local/bin/docker*` symlinks and credential helper can conflict with the new setup. Use Troubleshoot → Uninstall in the app, then delete `Docker.app`. Then edit `~/.docker/config.json` and remove `"credsStore": "desktop"` if it's there. If you leave it, every `docker pull` or `docker login` will fail.

2. **Install the packages:**
   ```bash
   brew install colima docker docker-compose docker-buildx
   ```

3. **Make `docker compose` (with a space) work, not just `docker-compose`.** Add this to `~/.docker/config.json`:
   ```json
   {
     "cliPluginsExtraDirs": ["/opt/homebrew/lib/docker/cli-plugins"]
   }
   ```
   If the file already has other keys, add this key alongside them.

## First run

```bash
# Start the VM: native arm64, VZ virtualization, Rosetta for any amd64 images, virtiofs mounts
colima start --vm-type vz --vz-rosetta --mount-type virtiofs --cpu 4 --memory 8 --disk 100

# Colima creates and selects a "colima" docker context automatically
docker context ls

# Check that it works
docker run --rm hello-world
docker run --rm alpine uname -m        # should print aarch64
docker compose version
docker buildx version
```

Then run `docker compose up` in one of your projects as usual.

## Daily use

- **Start and stop:** `colima start` and `colima stop`. The settings you used the first time are saved, and you can change them with `colima start --edit`.
- **Start at login (optional):** `brew services start colima`
- **Check status or troubleshoot:** `colima status`, `colima ssh`, `colima delete` (this wipes the VM)
- **amd64-only images:** `docker run --platform linux/amd64 ...` runs them through Rosetta.
- **Tools that expect `/var/run/docker.sock`** (Testcontainers, some IDEs): set this in your shell profile:
  ```bash
  export DOCKER_HOST="unix://$HOME/.colima/default/docker.sock"
  ```
  For Testcontainers, also set `TESTCONTAINERS_DOCKER_SOCKET_OVERRIDE=/var/run/docker.sock`.
- **Port forwarding:** this happens automatically, so `-p 8080:80` is reachable at `localhost:8080`.

## Alternatives (if Colima doesn't suit you)

| Option | License | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Rancher Desktop** | Apache-2.0 | Free, with a GUI. Choose the "dockerd (moby)" engine for full `docker` and `docker compose` compatibility. It's heavier because it bundles Kubernetes, which you can turn off. Good if your team wants a Docker Desktop-style app. |
| **Podman / Podman Desktop** | Apache-2.0 | Free and daemonless. It offers a Docker-compatible socket, but `podman compose` and Docker API compatibility have occasional rough edges, so it's less of a drop-in replacement. |
| Apple `container` | Apache-2.0 | Apple's own open-source tool. Its CLI isn't Docker-compatible and it has no Compose, so it doesn't meet your requirements. |
| OrbStack | Proprietary | Very good, but **not open source**, and commercial use requires a paid license. |

**Bottom line:** Colima keeps your current `docker` and `docker compose` workflow with the least change. Uninstall Docker Desktop, run the `brew install` line, add the plugin directory to your config, and run `colima start`.

The tool I checked ([source]) has no tested Docker Desktop replacement, so this advice comes from general knowledge, not from an install someone ran for you. Version details may have moved; check `colima version` and `brew info colima` before you depend on a specific flag.

## Why Colima
- **Free and open source (MIT).** Colima runs a small Linux VM with the real Docker Engine (Moby, Apache‑2.0) inside it. The `docker` CLI, Compose and Buildx you get from Homebrew are also Apache‑2.0, so the Docker Desktop license doesn't apply to them.
- **Works with your existing commands.** It creates a `colima` Docker context, so `docker build`, `docker run` and `docker compose up` work unchanged.
- **Runs arm64 natively.** On Apple silicon the VM is arm64, so arm64 images run natively. It can also run amd64 images through Rosetta if you need them.
- **Terminal only.** There's no GUI.

**My assumptions:** you have Homebrew installed, you're on macOS 13 or later (needed for the faster `vz` VM backend), and you're fine with removing Docker Desktop.

## Install

1. **Quit and uninstall Docker Desktop.** You can use the Troubleshoot → Uninstall option in its menu, or drag it to the Trash. This avoids conflicting `docker` binaries and makes it clear for compliance that you no longer use it.
2. **Install the tools:**
   ```sh
   brew install colima docker docker-compose docker-buildx
   ```
3. **Let the Docker CLI find the Compose and Buildx plugins.** Homebrew's install notes for these packages tell you to do this. Add the following to `~/.docker/config.json`, merging it with what's already there:
   ```json
   "cliPluginsExtraDirs": ["/opt/homebrew/lib/docker/cli-plugins"]
   ```
4. **Remove Docker Desktop's credential helper.** If `~/.docker/config.json` has a `"credsStore": "desktop"` line, delete it or change it to `"osxkeychain"`. If you leave it, `docker login` and pulls from private registries will fail once Docker Desktop is gone.

```sh

colima start --cpu 4 --memory 8 --disk 60 --vm-type vz --mount-type virtiofs --vz-rosetta

docker context ls                 # "colima" should be marked active
docker run --rm alpine uname -m   # should print: aarch64
docker compose version            # confirms the Compose plugin is found

```

- `colima stop` and `colima start` to stop and restart the VM.
- `colima status` to check it.
- `brew services start colima` to start it automatically at login.
- To change CPU or memory later, run `colima stop`, then `colima start` with new flags. If that doesn't apply them, `colima delete` and start again, but **that wipes your images and volumes**.

- **Tools that expect `/var/run/docker.sock`** (some IDEs, Testcontainers): Colima's socket is at `~/.colima/default/docker.sock`. Point them at it with:
  ```sh

  ```


```bash
bd list                       # 給人看的列表
```

pairs.question: q10
pairs.prompt: 我用 Markdown 寫中文技術文件，一個段落就是一整行。每次 git diff 都是整行紅綠，根本看不出改了哪幾個字。是不是要另外裝什麼 diff 工具？我在 Ubuntu 上，git 已經裝好了。
pairs.A:
# 不用另外裝工具，git 內建的 word diff 就能做到

要加的只有一個設定。git 有 `--word-diff` 和 `--color-words`，只顯示行內改動的部分。

但直接用在中文上沒有效果。git 預設用空白切詞，一整段中文中間沒有空白，會被當成一個「詞」，結果還是整段紅綠。所以要給它一個正則，**把每個中文字當成一個單位，英文單字保持完整**。

## 主要推薦：用 `--color-words` 加上自訂切詞規則

### 1. 先試一次（不用改任何設定）

在你的 repo 裡執行：

```bash
git diff --color-words='[A-Za-z0-9_]+|[^[:space:]]'
```

- `[A-Za-z0-9_]+`：英文、數字、變數名稱整個當成一個詞，例如 `config_file`
- `[^[:space:]]`：其他非空白字元各自算一個單位，所以每個中文字和標點都分開比對

輸出會是同一行裡只有改到的字變紅或變綠。如果終端機沒有顏色，或你想複製貼上，可以改用文字標記：

```bash
git diff --word-diff=plain --word-diff-regex='[A-Za-z0-9_]+|[^[:space:]]'
```

刪掉的字顯示成 `[-舊字-]`，新增的字顯示成 `{+新字+}`。

### 2. 只對 Markdown 套用，設定一次就好

在 repo 根目錄的 `.gitattributes` 加一行（沒有這個檔就新建）：

```
*.md diff=cjk
```

然後設定這個 `cjk` diff driver 的切詞規則：

```bash
git config --global diff.cjk.wordRegex '[A-Za-z0-9_]+|[^[:space:]]'
```

之後只要打 `git diff --color-words` 或 `git diff --word-diff`，`.md` 檔就會自動用這個規則，其他程式碼檔案不受影響。

### 3. 設一個短指令（可選）

git 沒有「預設開啟 word diff」的設定，所以通常用 alias：

```bash
git config --global alias.wdiff 'diff --color-words'
```

以後打 `git wdiff` 就可以了。`git wdiff --cached` 和 `git wdiff HEAD~1` 這類寫法照常能用。`git log -p --color-words` 和 `git show --color-words` 也一樣有效。

### 我假設的前提

- **系統 locale 是 UTF-8**。Ubuntu 預設是 `en_US.UTF-8` 或 `C.UTF-8`，通常沒問題。如果中文字被切成亂碼（例如出現 `<E4>` 這種位元組），用 `locale` 檢查一下，確認 `LANG` 結尾是 `.UTF-8`。
- 我沒有在你的機器上實際跑過這些指令，請以你那邊的輸出為準。

## 補充：另一個習慣上的做法

很多人寫中文 Markdown 會改成**一句一行**，也就是在 `。`、`？` 後面換行。Markdown 渲染時同一段落裡的單一換行不會變成斷行，結果看起來一樣，但 diff 天然就是逐句的，`git blame` 和 merge 衝突也會清楚很多。這可以和上面的 word diff 一起用。

## 如果之後想要更好看的介面

- **delta**（`sudo apt install git-delta`）：有並排顯示、語法高亮。不過它預設的行內比對對中文是以整段連續中文為單位，效果不如上面的 `--color-words`，所以只是錦上添花，不能取代上面的設定。
- **diff-highlight**：Ubuntu 的 git 套件附帶，在 `/usr/share/doc/git/contrib/diff-highlight`，需要先 `make` 才能用。它只標出前後相同部分中間的差異區段，適合一段只改一處的情況。

結論：先跑第 1 步那行指令看效果，滿意的話再做第 2、3 步，什麼都不用裝。

## 第一步：先試一次（不會改任何設定）

在你的 repo 裡執行：

```bash
git diff --word-diff=color --word-diff-regex='[A-Za-z0-9_]+|[^[:space:]]'
```

- `[A-Za-z0-9_]+`：英文單字、變數名稱保持整個詞比對，不會被拆成一個一個字母。
- `[^[:space:]]`：其他非空白字元（中文字、標點）每個字單獨比對。
- `--word-diff=color`：只用顏色標出刪掉和新增的字。如果你的終端機沒有顏色，或是要貼到別的地方，可以改成 `--word-diff=plain`，會顯示成 `[-刪除-]{+新增+}`。

**我的假設：** 你的系統語系是 UTF-8（Ubuntu 預設就是）。如果中文顯示成亂碼，或是比對結果怪怪的，先執行 `locale` 確認 `LC_CTYPE` 是不是類似 `zh_TW.UTF-8` 或 `en_US.UTF-8`。

## 第二步：設定成固定使用（只對 Markdown 生效）

1. 讓 git 用你的切字規則比對 `.md` 檔。這一行會寫進 `~/.gitconfig`：
   ```bash
   git config --global diff.markdown.wordRegex '[A-Za-z0-9_]+|[^[:space:]]'
   ```
2. 在 repo 根目錄的 `.gitattributes` 加上這一行（沒有這個檔就新建一個）：
   ```
   *.md diff=markdown
   ```
3. 設一個簡短的別名：
   ```bash
   git config --global alias.wd 'diff --word-diff=color'
   ```

設定好之後，平常就這樣用：

```bash
git wd                 # 還沒 stage 的改動
git wd --cached        # 已經 stage 的改動
git wd HEAD~1          # 跟上一個 commit 比
git log -p --word-diff=color   # 看歷史紀錄時也能逐字顯示
```

**驗證方法：** 隨便改一個長段落裡的兩三個字，執行 `git wd`。如果只有那幾個字變色，就設定成功了。

## 第三步（可選）：想要更好看的介面

如果你想要左右並排顯示、語法上色，可以考慮 **delta**。Ubuntu 24.04 以後可以用 `sudo apt install git-delta` 安裝。要注意兩件事：
- [source] 沒有驗證過 delta。
- delta 標示行內差異是靠它自己切詞，中文可能還是會一整串一起標起來。

所以要「準確看出改了哪幾個字」，還是上面的 `--word-diff-regex` 方法最可靠。delta 比較適合當作看程式碼時的外觀升級。

## 補充建議

如果文件是多人協作，可以考慮改用「一句一行」的寫法：每個句號後面換行。Markdown 顯示時會自動合併成同一段，這樣以後連一般的 `git diff`、GitHub 的 PR 頁面都能清楚看出改了哪幾句。

pairs.prompt: On my Apple silicon MacBook Pro I want to run local LLMs with Apple's MLX framework instead of GGUF/llama.cpp, from the terminal only, behind a local OpenAI-compatible server that my coding tools can call, with streaming, since my editor streams responses. I recommend **`mlx-lm`**, Apple's own MLX package, which includes a built-in server called `mlx_lm.server`. It's MIT-licensed, terminal-only and needs no account. It provides OpenAI-style endpoints (`/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/models`) and streams when a request includes `"stream": true`. `--model` accepts either a Hugging Face repo ID (downloaded and cached on first use) or a local folder.

## Assumptions
- You have a native arm64 Python 3.10 or newer, not one running under Rosetta, and a recent macOS. Check with `python3 -c "import platform; print(platform.machine())"`, which should print `arm64`.
- You want a single-user server bound to localhost. The project says this server "is not recommended for production" because it has only basic security checks, so don't expose it to your network.

## Install
Either of these keeps it in its own isolated environment:
```bash
# Option A: uv (recommended)
brew install uv            # or: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
uv tool install mlx-lm

# Option B: pipx
brew install pipx && pipx ensurepath
pipx install mlx-lm
```
(Running `pip install mlx-lm` inside a venv also works.)

1. **Optional: try generation first.** This downloads the model the first time:
   ```bash

   ```
   Most quantized MLX models are under the `mlx-community` org on Hugging Face. As a rough guide, 4-bit 7–14B models suit 16–32 GB of RAM, and larger models need more.

2. **Start the server:**
   ```bash
   mlx_lm.server --model mlx-community/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-4bit --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
   # or a local folder:
   mlx_lm.server --model ~/models/my-mlx-model
   ```
   It listens on localhost:8080 by default. Run `mlx_lm.server --help` to see all options, such as KV-cache quantization with `--kv-bits`.

3. **Test streaming** from a second terminal:
   ```bash
   curl -N http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hi"}],"stream":true,"max_tokens":50}'
   ```
   You should see `chat.completion.chunk` events arriving one at a time.

4. **Point your editor or tools at the server:**
   - Base URL: `http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1`
   - API key: any placeholder string, such as `local`, if the tool requires one
   - Model name: the same repo ID or path you passed to `--model`. `GET /v1/models` lists what's available.

## Tips
- To convert or quantize your own model: `mlx_lm.convert --hf-path <repo> -q`. This writes a local folder that you can pass to `--model`.
- Downloads are cached in `~/.cache/huggingface`. You can change the location with `HF_HOME`.
- It handles one user well. If you need concurrent requests from several tools, look at the alternatives below.

## Alternatives (also free, terminal-only)
- **mlx-omni-server**: an MLX server that implements more of the OpenAI API, including tools/function calling and embeddings. It's worth trying if your coding tool depends on tool calls.
- **vllm-mlx**: a vLLM-style MLX server built for batching and concurrent requests.

Both are community projects and change more often than `mlx-lm`, so check their READMEs before installing.

pairs.question: q13
pairs.prompt: We run Ollama on a CPU-only Linux server (no GPU, 64 GB RAM) for about 10 teammates, and it slows to a crawl when several people send requests at once. I already have a folder of GGUF files from Hugging Face and don't want them copied into Ollama's own model store. What free, open-source server can load GGUF files directly from a path, handle concurrent requests efficiently on CPU, and expose an OpenAI-compatible API?

# My recommendation: llama.cpp's `llama-server`

**`llama-server` from llama.cpp** (MIT license) does what you need:

- **Loads a GGUF from any path** with `-m /path/to/model.gguf`. Nothing gets copied or imported.
- **Handles many users at once on CPU.** It splits the context into N parallel slots (`-np`) and batches them together. On CPU, generating each token is limited mostly by memory bandwidth. Batching lets several users share one pass over the model weights, so 8 requests at once cost much less than 8 requests one after another.
- **OpenAI-compatible API**: `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/completions`, `/v1/embeddings` and `/v1/models`, with streaming and an optional API key. It also includes a simple web chat UI.
- It's the engine Ollama is built on, so your GGUFs will work as-is and you'll be closer to the newest CPU optimizations.

**What I assumed:** an x86_64 Linux server, one main shared model, and teammates who connect over the LAN.

## Install (choose one)

**A. Prebuilt binary (simplest)**
1. From https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases, download the latest `…-bin-ubuntu-x64` archive.
2. Extract it into its own directory, for example `/opt/llama.cpp/`. `llama-server` is inside.

**B. Build from source (tuned to your CPU's AVX2/AVX-512 support)**
```bash
sudo apt install -y build-essential cmake git
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp
cd llama.cpp
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build -j"$(nproc)"
# binary: build/bin/llama-server
```

**C. Docker**: `ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server`, with your GGUF folder mounted read-only (`-v /data/gguf:/models:ro`).

## First run
```bash
./llama-server \
  -m /data/gguf/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 \
  -np 8 -c 32768 \
  -t $(nproc --ignore=2) \
  --api-key "change-me" \
  --metrics
```
- `-np 8` gives 8 parallel slots. Requests beyond 8 wait in a queue instead of slowing everyone down.
- `-c 32768` is the total context across all slots, so each slot gets about 4K tokens. If people need longer prompts, raise `-c` or lower `-np`.
- For `-t`, use the number of **physical** cores. Hyperthreads usually don't help.
- Flag defaults change between releases, so check `./llama-server --help` against your build.

**Test it:**
```bash
curl http://SERVER:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer change-me" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"any","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}]}'
```
Teammates set their OpenAI client's base URL to `http://SERVER:8080/v1` and use the key. To keep it running permanently, wrap the command in a systemd unit.

## Tips for CPU-only serving
- **Model size matters more than anything else.** A 7–8B model at Q4_K_M will feel responsive for about 10 users. A 30B+ dense model will be slow on any CPU server, whatever the software. Mixture-of-experts models, like the Qwen3-30B-A3B class, are often a good fit for CPU with 64 GB of RAM.
- **Serving several models from your folder:** add **llama-swap** (also open source). It sits in front of `llama-server` and starts the right model based on the `model` field in each request, still reading from your paths.
- **If you'd rather keep Ollama for now:** setting `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` and `OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE` may reduce the slowdown. But it still wants its own model store, and `llama-server` gives you more direct control.

- **Xyntetik Runner:** it serves GGUF over an OpenAI-compatible API, but its handling of many users on CPU wasn't tested.
- **SunnyNet:** it only supports GGUF for RWKV-style models, and its API wasn't tested.

# Recommendation: llama.cpp's `llama-server`

Use **`llama-server` from llama.cpp** (MIT license). Ollama is built on the same engine, so you'll get the same inference speed. The difference is that you control concurrency directly.

- **Loads GGUF from any path.** `-m /path/to/model.gguf` reads the file where it is. Nothing is copied or converted.
- **Handles concurrent requests on CPU.** It splits the server into several request slots with `--parallel N` and uses continuous batching, which is on by default. Requests from different people are combined into one forward pass instead of waiting in line. On CPU, generating each token is mostly limited by memory bandwidth, so batching 4–8 users raises total tokens per second a lot compared with serving them one at a time.
- **OpenAI-compatible API.** It serves `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/completions`, `/v1/embeddings` and `/v1/models`, plus a built-in web chat UI. It also supports optional `--api-key` auth.

**Assumptions:** an x86-64 Linux server and models in the 7B–32B range. I haven't checked the current release for exact flag names, so confirm them with `llama-server --help`.

## Install (pick one)

**A. Prebuilt binary (simplest)**
1. Go to https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases.
2. Download the `llama-<build>-bin-ubuntu-x64.zip` asset (the CPU build) and unzip it, for example to `/opt/llama.cpp`.
3. Check it runs: `/opt/llama.cpp/llama-server --version`

**B. Docker**
```bash
docker run -d --name llama -p 8080:8080 \
  -v /srv/gguf:/models:ro \
  ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server \
  -m /models/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 -c 32768 -np 4 -t 16
```
The `:ro` mount keeps your GGUF folder read-only and in place.

**C. Build from source (best CPU tuning, since it compiles for your exact CPU)**
```bash
sudo apt install -y build-essential cmake git libcurl4-openssl-dev
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DGGML_NATIVE=ON
cmake --build build -j --target llama-server
# binary: build/bin/llama-server
```

## First run
```bash
llama-server \
  -m /srv/gguf/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 \
  -np 4 \                 # 4 concurrent request slots
  -c 32768 \              # TOTAL context, divided across slots (~8k each here)
  -t 16 \                 # = number of PHYSICAL cores, not hyperthreads
  -a team-model \         # model name clients will use
  --api-key "change-me"
```

Test it:
```bash
curl http://SERVER:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer change-me" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"team-model","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}]}'
```
To point existing clients at it, set the base URL to `http://SERVER:8080/v1` and the API key to `change-me`.

## Tuning for 10 users on CPU
- **`-np`:** start at 4. Try 6–8 if replies stay fast enough. More slots give more total throughput, but each user's stream gets slower.
- **`-c`:** this is shared across all slots. For example, 8 slots × 8k tokens means `-c 65536`. The KV cache uses RAM, so check memory use after changing it.
- **`-t`:** set it to physical cores (`lscpu`: cores per socket × sockets). Going above that usually makes things slower. On dual-socket servers, also try `--numa distribute`.
- **Model size matters more than anything else.** On CPU, a 7–14B model at Q4_K_M is responsive for a team. 32B+ will feel slow under load no matter which server you use.
- **Watch it with `/metrics`** (enable with `--metrics`) or `/slots` to see whether requests are queuing.
- **Keep it running** under a systemd unit with `Restart=always` that wraps the command above.

## Several models from one folder
A single `llama-server` process normally serves one model. You have two options:
- **Router mode:** recent builds can point at a whole folder with `--models-dir /srv/gguf` and load models on demand, picked by the request's `model` field. Check `--help` for your build, since this feature is newer.
- **llama-swap** (https://github.com/mostlygeek/llama-swap, MIT): a small proxy that starts and stops `llama-server` per model, still reading files from your folder.

Either way, keep only 1–2 models loaded at once. Every loaded model takes RAM and CPU from the others.

## Other options I considered
- **Tune Ollama instead:** `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4` and `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS=1` may fix much of the slowdown. But importing GGUF into Ollama (`FROM /path` in a Modelfile) copies the file into its blob store, which you said you want to avoid.
- **LocalAI:** also open source and OpenAI-compatible, and it uses llama.cpp underneath. It's heavier, and its main benefit is supporting more kinds of models.
- **vLLM (CPU build):** strong batching, but its GGUF support is experimental and its CPU path is weaker. Not a good fit here.
- **KoboldCpp:** loads GGUF from a path, but it's aimed at single users and handles concurrency less well.

**Bottom line:** run `llama-server` with `-np 4–8`, `-t` set to your physical cores, and a mid-sized Q4 model. Add router mode or llama-swap if you need to switch between models.

pairs.question: q14
pairs.prompt: I'm building a small RAG tool for internal use at my company on a CPU-only Linux box (8 GB RAM, no GPU) and want to stop sending documents to cloud APIs. I need one local, open-source server that gives me both an OpenAI-compatible /v1/embeddings endpoint and a rerank endpoint, with models that handle mixed English and Chinese documents and whose licenses allow commercial use. What should I run?
pairs.A:
I'd run **[Infinity](https://github.com/michaelfeil/infinity)**, using the MIT-licensed Python **v2** server and its CPU Docker image, with two models:

- **Embeddings:** `BAAI/bge-m3` (MIT license, strong on mixed Chinese and English, handles inputs up to 8k tokens)
- **Rerank:** `BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3` (Apache-2.0, multilingual, built to pair with bge-m3)

One Infinity process can serve several models. It gives you an OpenAI-compatible `/v1/embeddings` endpoint and a `/v1/rerank` endpoint (Cohere/Jina style), and both models fit in 8 GB of RAM.

**Use v2, not v3.** The new native **v3** server, released in late October, puts its new code under a custom "Infinity Restricted MIT License" with restrictions on providers. The Python `infinity-emb` package and the `infinity_emb v2` command are still plain MIT. For an internal commercial tool, stick with v2 unless your legal team clears v3.

## Install and first run

I'm assuming an x86-64 Linux box with Docker installed, and internet access for the first model download only.

```bash
# 1. Make a folder to cache the models (~4.5 GB download the first time)
mkdir -p ~/infinity-cache

# 2. Start the server. Pin a specific *-cpu tag from Docker Hub (michaelf34/infinity) rather than latest-cpu.
docker run -d --name infinity --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 127.0.0.1:7997:7997 \
  -v ~/infinity-cache:/app/.cache \
  michaelf34/infinity:latest-cpu \
  v2 --engine torch \
     --model-id BAAI/bge-m3 \
     --model-id BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 \
     --batch-size 8 --batch-size 8 \
     --url-prefix /v1 \
     --port 7997

# 3. Watch the logs until both models are loaded
docker logs -f infinity
```

Smoke tests:

```bash
# Embeddings (OpenAI format)
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7997/v1/embeddings -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"BAAI/bge-m3","input":["How do I file an expense report?","如何提交报销单？"]}' | head -c 300

# Rerank
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7997/v1/rerank -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3","query":"报销流程","documents":["Expense reports are filed in Concur.","午餐菜单在这里。"]}'

# The full API reference is at http://127.0.0.1:7997/docs
```

To use it from code, point the OpenAI SDK at it: `OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:7997/v1", api_key="unused")`, then call `client.embeddings.create(model="BAAI/bge-m3", input=[...])`. Rerank is a plain HTTP POST as shown above. LangChain and LlamaIndex both have Infinity integrations.

If you'd rather skip Docker: `pip install "infinity-emb[all]"`, then run `infinity_emb v2 ...` with the same flags.

## Tips for 8 GB, CPU only

- **Memory:** each model is about 568M parameters, roughly 2.2 GB in fp32, so about 5 GB total. Keep batch sizes small (4–8) and leave headroom for the OS and your app.
- **Speed:** indexing is the slow part on CPU. Chunk documents to about 300–512 tokens instead of using bge-m3's full 8k, and rerank only the top 20–50 results. Bulk indexing will take a while, but query-time latency should be fine.
- **Staying offline:** once the models are cached, add `-e HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1` so the server never contacts Hugging Face again.
- **Security:** the server has no authentication by default. Keep it bound to localhost (as above) or put it behind a reverse proxy. Check `infinity_emb v2 --help` for an `--api-key` option.

## Alternatives

- **[Hugging Face Text Embeddings Inference (TEI)](https://github.com/huggingface/text-embeddings-inference)** (Apache-2.0, actively maintained, CPU image around `cpu-1.8.x`): native `/v1/embeddings` and `/rerank`, and very fast on CPU. The catch is that it serves one model per instance, so you'd run two containers on different ports with the same two models. Choose this if being actively maintained matters more to you than having a single process.
- **Lighter or newer models:** `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B` and `Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B` (Apache-2.0) are also very good at Chinese. Server support for the Qwen3 reranker varies, though, so try it before switching.
- **Licenses to avoid:** jina-embeddings-v3 and jina-reranker-v2 are CC-BY-NC, which doesn't allow commercial use.

Sources:
- [Infinity GitHub](https://github.com/michaelfeil/infinity)
- [Infinity v3.0.0 release notes (licensing, CPU image)](https://github.com/michaelfeil/infinity/releases/tag/v3.0.0)
- [Text Embeddings Inference GitHub](https://GitHub.com/huggingface/text-embeddings-inference)

## Recommendation: Xinference (Apache-2.0) serving bge-m3 and bge-reranker-v2-m3

Xinference is the simplest way to get both endpoints from **one server process**:

- **Embeddings:** `POST /v1/embeddings` (OpenAI-compatible)
- **Rerank:** `POST /v1/rerank` (body: `model`, `query`, `documents`, `top_n`; Cohere/Jina-style)
- It has an official **CPU Docker image** (`xprobe/xinference:latest-cpu`).
- It's built by a Chinese team, so English+Chinese models are a core use case.

**Models (licenses allow commercial use):**

| Role | Model | License | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Embeddings | `BAAI/bge-m3` | MIT | Strong in Chinese and English, 8k context, 1024-dim |
| Rerank | `BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3` | Apache-2.0 | Same model family, built for multiple languages |

**Avoid** `jina-embeddings-v3` and `jina-reranker-v2`. They're CC-BY-NC, which doesn't allow commercial use. Check each model's license on its Hugging Face card before you deploy.

**RAM assumption:** Both models are about 570M parameters and run in full precision on CPU. Together with Xinference's own overhead, expect roughly **5–6 GB**. That fits in 8 GB, but not with much room to spare. If memory gets tight, see the fallbacks below.

### Install and first run (Docker assumed)

```bash
# 1. Start the server; the volume keeps downloaded models across restarts
docker run -d --name xinference -p 9997:9997 \
  -v $HOME/xinference:/root/.xinference \
  -v $HOME/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  xprobe/xinference:latest-cpu \
  xinference-local --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9997
# (If Hugging Face is slow or blocked from your network, add: -e XINFERENCE_MODEL_SRC=modelscope)

# 2. Load the two models (they download on first launch)
docker exec xinference xinference launch --model-name bge-m3 --model-type embedding \
  --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:9997
docker exec xinference xinference launch --model-name bge-reranker-v2-m3 --model-type rerank \
  --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:9997

# 3. Test embeddings (OpenAI-compatible)
curl http://localhost:9997/v1/embeddings -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"bge-m3","input":["报销流程是什么？","What is the expense process?"]}'

# 4. Test rerank
curl http://localhost:9997/v1/rerank -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"bge-reranker-v2-m3","query":"报销流程",
       "documents":["Expense reports are filed in the HR portal.","午餐菜单每周更新。"],"top_n":2}'
```

**In your app:** point the OpenAI SDK at `base_url="http://<host>:9997/v1"` with any dummy API key, and call `/v1/rerank` directly. Models aren't reloaded automatically after a container restart, so put the two `launch` commands in a startup script. Once the models are cached, nothing leaves the machine. If you set `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`, it also stops checking Hugging Face for updates.

## Fallbacks

1. **llama.cpp `llama-server` (MIT): the lowest-RAM option.** It serves `/v1/embeddings` and `/v1/rerank` from 8-bit GGUF versions of the same two models, at roughly 600 MB each. The catch is one model per process, so you'd run two processes on two ports (for example, `llama-server -m bge-m3-Q8_0.gguf --embedding --port 8081` and `llama-server -m bge-reranker-v2-m3-Q8_0.gguf --reranking --port 8082`). Choose this if Xinference uses too much memory.
2. **Hugging Face Text Embeddings Inference (Apache-2.0).** It's fast and lightweight on CPU (`ghcr.io/huggingface/text-embeddings-inference:cpu-<version>`; the newest tag I found was `cpu-1.8.1`). It also serves only one model per container, so you'd need two containers. Its rerank route is `/rerank`, not `/v1/rerank`. To my knowledge it also has an OpenAI-style `/v1/embeddings` route, but I didn't confirm that here, so check the `/docs` page once it's running.
3. **Smaller models if you stay on Xinference:** `Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B` and `Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B` (both Apache-2.0, very good at Chinese). Neither of these is much smaller than the bge pair, though. To actually save RAM, swap in a smaller reranker such as `bge-reranker-base`.

**Why not Infinity:** Its newer v3 server uses a custom "Infinity Restricted MIT" license, and for company use that needs a legal review first. **Why not Ollama:** it has no rerank endpoint.

# 建議：whisper.cpp + OpenCC 轉繁體

最推薦的組合是 **whisper.cpp**（純 C/C++，不需要 PyTorch）加上 **OpenCC**（簡轉繁）。兩者都免費、開源、完全離線。

**為什麼選這個組合：**
- **不用 PyTorch**：whisper.cpp 編譯完只有幾 MB，模型檔另外下載。large-v3-turbo 量化版大約 550 MB，比裝好幾 GB 的 PyTorch 小很多。
- **CPU 上比較快**：在 CPU 上通常比 openai-whisper 快好幾倍，主要靠 SIMD/AVX、多執行緒和量化模型。large-v3-turbo 的解碼層比 large-v3 少很多，準確度接近，速度快很多。實際速度要看你的 CPU。
- **可以直接輸出 SRT**：加 `-osrt` 就會產生含時間軸的字幕檔。
- **繁體輸出穩定**：Whisper 的中文訓練資料以簡體居多，加提示詞（prompt）可以提高輸出繁體的機率，但不保證。最穩的做法是轉完再用 OpenCC 轉一次。OpenCC 只改字，不會動 SRT 的時間軸。

**我的假設：** 你用 Ubuntu/Debian 系的發行版、x86_64 CPU，錄音是普通話會議。下面的指令我沒有在你的電腦上執行過，請先確認內容再跑。

## 安裝

```bash
# 1. 編譯工具、ffmpeg、OpenCC（需要 sudo）
sudo apt install build-essential cmake git ffmpeg opencc

# 2. 下載並編譯 whisper.cpp
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp
cd whisper.cpp
cmake -B build
cmake --build build -j --config Release

# 3. 下載模型（建議先試 turbo 量化版，兼顧速度與準確度）

# 太慢的話可以改用 small 或 medium，速度快但錯字較多

# 4.（選用）下載 VAD 模型：跳過靜音段，可以減少「幻聽」重複句
sh ./models/download-vad-model.sh silero-v5.1.2
```

## 第一次執行

```bash
# 1. 轉成 whisper.cpp 需要的格式：16 kHz、單聲道 WAV
ffmpeg -i meeting.m4a -ar 16000 -ac 1 -c:a pcm_s16le meeting.wav

# 2. 轉錄並輸出 SRT（-t 填你的 CPU 實體核心數）
./build/bin/whisper-cli \
  -m models/ggml-large-v3-turbo-q5_0.bin \
  -f meeting.wav \
  -l zh -t 8 \
  --prompt "以下是繁體中文的會議逐字稿。" \
  --vad -vm models/ggml-silero-v5.1.2.bin \
  -osrt -of meeting
# 產生 meeting.srt（沒有下載 VAD 模型的話，拿掉 --vad 那一行）

# 3. 轉成台灣繁體，s2twp 會連用語一起轉，例如 软件→軟體、视频→影片
opencc -i meeting.srt -o meeting.zh-TW.srt -c s2twp.json
```

- 只想轉字、不想改用語的話，把 `s2twp.json` 換成 `s2tw.json`。

- 可以把會議常出現的人名和專有名詞寫進 `--prompt`，辨識會比較準。

1. **whisper-ctranslate2（底層是 faster-whisper）**
   - 用 CTranslate2 引擎，同樣不需要 PyTorch，CPU 上用 int8 也很快。

   ```bash

     --compute_type int8 --vad_filter True \
     --initial_prompt "以下是繁體中文的會議逐字稿。" --output_format srt
   ```
